catalog_locator: sec. 1.2 Phonotactics and sec. 1.3 Stress, pp. 297-298 (scanned)
catalog_quote: Closed syllables are infrequent, under 1% of the total. The final consonant in CVC syllables is always a nasal, and the only consonant clusters in the language involve these syllable-final nasals. 1.3 Stress Stress does not carry contrastive meaning. The penultimate vowel in a word is stressed, with secondary stress on preceding alternate vowels. The exception occurs with word-final CVC syllables in which the ultimate vowel carries the stress; there is evidence which suggests that in these cases there is an underlying word-final /i/ or /u/ which has been dropped. When suffixing occurs, the stress transfers to the penultimate vowel in the suffixed form. In a word-final sequence of two vowels, if the first vowel is higher than the second, then the sequence consists of two syllables; otherwise, the sequence results in a single syllable.

audit.reasoning: (1) Quote check: confirmed verbatim at the stated locator in the excerpt file we hold and in the full-sketch scanned (lines 74-80); the domain quotation and exq_ likewise verbatim; nothing elsewhere in the 25-page sketch contradicts (only other stress mention, sec. 3.2, is consistent with stress shift under suffixation). (2) Deciding source: a 2002 first-hand grammar sketch by the long-term SIL fieldworker, published in the standard Oceanic reference volume. Glottolog's 'grammar' entry (674593) is a duplicate record of this same chapter, so no fuller grammar exists; the only other descriptive works are the same authors' 1992 Field Notes (x+142 pp) and 2008 Organised Phonology Data. No database (WALS 14A-17A checked locally: none) codes Gapapaiwa stress, and I know of no instrumental/JIPA/dissertation work on its prosody.
